By the end of this lesson I will be able to

The big ideaIn science, PURE means only ONE substance: one element or one compound. A pure substance melts and boils at one fixed temperature.

Notes

In shops, "pure" often means "nothing added", like "100% pure orange juice". In science, PURE means something different: a pure substance is made of only ONE substance. Orange juice is not pure in science, because it contains water, sugar, vitamins and many other substances.

STEP 2 · EXPLORE

Pure and impure

8 – 18 min · Task 2 · Criterion A
  • A pure substance contains only one type of particle. It can be an element (gold, oxygen) or a compound (pure water, pure salt).
  • An impure substance has other substances mixed in. These extra substances are called impurities.
  • Impure substances are mixtures. Examples: tap water, sea water, air, soil, juice, milk.

Notes

If a drop of water evaporates, any dissolved solids are left behind as a residue (a mark). Pure water leaves no residue; impure water leaves a ring or white mark. Samples: A = distilled water, B = tap water, C = salt water. Put 3 drops of each next to its letter on a clean mirror or black tile, leave them under a lamp or in the sun for 10–15 minutes, then look closely.

STEP 4 · EXPLAIN

Melting and boiling points

38 – 50 min · Task 4 · Criterion A
  • A pure substance melts and boils at ONE fixed temperature. Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C (at sea level).
  • Impurities change these temperatures: salt water boils ABOVE 100 °C and freezes BELOW 0 °C.
  • An impure substance often melts over a RANGE of temperatures, not at one exact temperature.
  • Scientists test melting or boiling points to check whether a substance is pure.
